bio.en: Christopher Lochhead is a three-time public company CMO, advisor to 50+ venture-backed startups, and the "Godfather of Category Design" — a 13-time number-one bestselling co-author (Play Bigger, Niche Down, The 22 Laws of Category Design) and co-creator of the Substack Category Pirates.
bio.zh: Christopher Lochhead 是一位三度任职上市公司 CMO、50 多家风投初创的顾问，以及"品类设计教父"——13 次登上榜首的畅销书合著者（《Play Bigger》《Niche Down》《品类设计 22 律》）和 Substack《Category Pirates》的联合创作者。

summary.en: Christopher makes the case that legendary companies design new categories rather than compete in existing ones: in tech categories, one company captures ~two-thirds of the total value, so competing means fighting for the remaining 24%. He explains category design as framing, naming, and claiming a problem (not just shipping a "better" product), and warns the "better trap" (Threads, Amazon Fire Phone, Red Bull Cola) fails because problems create categories, not vice versa. Practical tools include backcasting (envision the future, then work backward), "reject the premise," strategic languaging (e.g., Otis's "vertical railway," Starbucks's new vocabulary, OpenAI's "LLM"), targeting super-consumers, and the lightning-strike model of marketing powered by word of mouth. He also argues positioning and "product market fit" are dangerously incremental mind-sets.
summary.zh: Christopher 提出论点：传奇公司设计新品类、而不是在已有品类里竞争——在科技品类里，一家公司拿走总价值约三分之二，所以竞争意味着为剩下 24% 打架。他把品类设计解释为框定、命名并主张一个问题（不只是发布一个"更好"的产品），并警告"更好"陷阱（Threads、Amazon Fire Phone、Red Bull Cola）会失败，因为问题造就品类，而非反过来。实用工具包括 backcasting（构想未来再倒推）、"reject the premise"、战略性语言化（如 Otis 的"垂直铁路"、星巴克的新词汇、OpenAI 的"LLM"）、瞄准超级消费者，以及由口碑驱动的闪电袭击营销模型。他还主张定位和"产品市场契合"是危险的渐进式思维。

Okay, turns out that while that's highly effective for a hike, it is intergalactic disaster for a startup. Here's why. Your point of reference is everything. Thinking about thinking is the most important kind of thinking. (01:03:59): When we do it that way, mentally we are standing in the present, which is an extension of the past, and we're saying, "What do we need to do to go from this present to the different future we want, and what are the obstacles in the way?" Here's the mental scaffolding. That's forecasting, here's backcasting. (01:04:26): We do an exercise, we abandon everything. In category design you get taught to what's called reject the premise, so I reject everything about the way that it is, all of it. You and I now envision this future five years out and everything's gone incredibly, it's exceeded our expectations. We make that true in our minds. We write out, we brainstorm out "What's it going to be like? What kind of technology are we selling? What are we doing for customers? How big's our company? How many people will hire?" Da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da. Then we say, "Okay, standing in that future, five years out, looking back to the present, what did we do to make this different future happen?" That's category design. That's how you unshackle yourself from the past. See, one of the biggest disservices in our industry is this word disrupt. "Oh, [inaudible 01:05:26] we're going to go disrupt the engineering industry." Nah. Well, if you're disrupting something, by definition, your reference point is the something. And when your reference point is an existing thing, your reference point is the past. If we want to be able to think in unconstrained ways about a radically different future, the more we drag the past forward, the worse off we are. What reject the premise teaches us is let's forget everything we know and start fresh. My friend, a legendary designer, John Bielenberg, does this course on innovation and design with kids in university. He does this multi-week exercise and the objective of the exercise, Lenny, is design a bicycle. That's the objective. And there's only one design point. It cannot be rideable. (01:06:25): And the reason John makes him do that, his philosophy, he calls it thinking wrong. That's his version, if you will, of reject the premise. The reason for it is when you take away the premise, it must be rideable, you open up the aperture for legendary new thinking, radically different possibilities, radically different futures. This is the mistake that many, many entrepreneurs make, is whether they realize it or not, what they're doing is incremental better and they're fighting for market share, fighting for existing demand with something that's incrementally better. And the reality is that's why most entrepreneurs fail. Now, you could fail doing it exponentially different, it sounds medically insane to say "What you want is a zero billion dollars market." However, as crazy as it sounds, it's the only thing that leads to meaningful success. And the proof is in the data.

turns.en: There's a bunch of these product myths. Product led growth is another one, but let's go to product market fit. And God bless Mark Andreessen, he's the guy that framed it. (01:12:43): Okay, well, Threads achieved product market fit faster than any product in the history of the world. Here's the aha, categories make products not the other way around. But one of the things we wanted to understand is what categories of business books sold and which categories didn't and why. We can get into all that if you want, but here's the aha. Guess what the number one category of business books, nonfiction books is by a mile.
turns.zh: 有一堆这种产品迷思。产品驱动增长是另一个，但我们去产品市场契合。愿 Mark Andreessen 安好，他是框定它的人。而 Kevin 刚写了篇真深思的帖子讲为什么它是倒的，如果你要我乐意发你。Kevin Maney，天才。这是 aha，再次，品类设计原则。听那些词，产品、市场、契合。产品市场契合。现在，让我想，对我能做的，是找个方式把我的产品 fit 进一个市。（01:11:48）挺简单的方式去确定或提炼产品市场契合。而产品市场契合变成的意思是，我们是个 brew pub，你我想开个精酿啤酒地方像西海岸其他所有人，而我们要做一堆样本和 shit，而我们要喂那些样本给我们的朋友和我的理想客户画像——我从 Lenny 学的。而如果足够多我朋友圈和理想客户群里的人说"那是个美味 IPA，我喜欢，"然后我们要建它。然后如果人们开始买那个 IPA，我们有，而这些是人们用的词，"达成产品市场契合。"（01:12:43）好，嗯，Threads 比世界史上任何产品更快达成产品市场契合。这是 aha，品类造就产品，不是反过来。你要的是为你的产品设计市场品类，而不是把你的产品 fit 进一个市场品类。而问题是，我们行业，像很多其他，但科技行业，满是产品偏执狂，因为他们真真真真真相信，像他们相信氧气的可得性，最好的产品赢。他们真信。而他们相信营销的工作是"你能在我们网站放个 demo、拿个 demo 吗？我们能有个病毒视频是 demo 吗？因为一旦人们看到我们东西多好、多快、多便宜、多小、多大，随便，他们会买，"而他们不。他们买的是对一个需要不同方案的问/机会的新洞察。那是他们买的。这是另一个简单例子。这是我现在常听到的，"我们需要的是个故事，我们需要个故事品牌。作为初创创始人你在营销里能做的头号事是分享你的初创创始人旅程。分享你的旅程。"这是所有我们听到的 shit。我们听一阵了。嗯，猜怎么着？没人在乎你的旅程。他们真不在乎。你知道他们在乎什么？他们自己。他们的问题、他们的需求、他们的机会。为我们的书《Snow Leopard》，我们做了史上第一个用 Nielsen 数据做的综合数据科学研究去研究非虚构书。而我们知道因为 Nielsen 告诉我们的，而我们得签个能噎死马的 NDA 关于我们能说不能说什么关于数据。但我们想懂的一件事是什么品类商业书卖、什么不卖、为什么。我们能进所有那些如果你要，但这是 aha。猜什么商业书头号品类、非虚构书，遥遥领先。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh my god. Sales? Marketing, marketing-sales. No.
turns.zh: 哦我的天。销售？营销、营销-销售。不。

turns.speaker: Christopher Lochhead
turns.en: Personal growth.
turns.zh: 个人成长。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, that makes sense. Self-help.
turns.zh: 好，那说得通。自助。

turns.speaker: Christopher Lochhead
turns.en: Self-help. And number two, personal finance. Biographies are way down on the list. The point being, no one cares about our product. No one cares that it's 25 mega flips faster, cheaper, whatever, they don't care. You know what they care about? Them, their needs, their wants, their problems. And categories are about customers and their wants, needs, problems and opportunities. Branding and marketing is about our product. And the greatest innovators in the world don't stop at innovating a product or technology. They design a new innovative market category where they standalone.
turns.zh: 自助。而第二，个人理财。传记在清单很下面。点是，没人在乎我们的产品。没人在乎它快 25 兆倍、更便宜、随便，他们不在乎。你知道他们在乎什么？他们自己、他们的需求、他们的想要、他们的问题。而品类是关于客户和他们的想要、需求、问题、机会。品牌和营销是关于我们的产品。而世界上最伟大的创新者不停在创新一个产品或技术。他们设计一个他们独占的新创新市场品类。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We're definitely going along, which I expected. And we've actually gone through most of the questions I had, but I have just a few more to close out the conversation. One is positioning. That's something you hear a lot about. How do you think about positioning versus categorying? Are they essentially the same thing? Is positioning just a way to phrase and describe your category? How should people think about that?
turns.zh: 我们绝对顺着走，我预期到了。而我们其实走完我大多问题，但我只剩几个收尾。一个是定位（positioning）。那是你常听到的。你怎么想定位 vs 品类化（categorying）？它们本质一样吗？定位只是个表述和描述你品类的方式？人们该怎么想那个？

turns.speaker: Christopher Lochhead
turns.en: What positioning today has become is essentially how do I tell a story about my shit in a unique way, in a compelling way? That's really what people mean when they say positioning. The parts they never stop to consider, again, listen to the words positioning as it relates to what? Because you, again, listen to the words and fucking think, "You position against competitors." How do we position against the competitors? That's a phrase people use. The question is, what are you positioning against? And the answer to that question almost all of the time is competition. If you're doing positioning in that context, you just decided you're fighting for 24% of the demand designed by somebody else. And we think in the tech space where one company earns two thirds of the economics, if that's your starting point, you fuck yourself from the start. To put it simply, positioning in the modern context is for losers. That is to say people who are fighting over the 24%. That's positioning.
turns.zh: 今天的定位变成本质是我怎么用独特方式、吸引人方式讲个关于我的 shit 的故事？那真的是人们说定位时的意思。他们从不停下来考虑的部份，再次，听那些词定位关于什么？因为你，再次，听那些词、操去想"你针对竞品定位。"我们怎么针对竞品定位？那是人们用的短语。问题是，你针对什么定位？而那个问题的答案几乎总是竞争。如果你在那个语境做定位，你刚决定你在为别人设计的 24% 需求打架。而我们认为在科技空间一家公司赚三分之二经济，如果那是你的起点，你从一开始 fuck 自己。简单说，现代语境的定位是给 loser 的。也就是那些为 24% 打架的人。那是定位。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love it. Getting spicy over here.
turns.zh: 我爱。在这变辣了。

turns.speaker: Christopher Lochhead
turns.en: Well, it's factually correct. People go, "Oh, [inaudible 01:18:21]." Okay, so you mean to tell me that in tech one company doesn't take two thirds of the economics? Okay, believe that. And you can believe gravity doesn't exist. It does, but you can believe that Bigfoots are installing misters on 5G towers to make us all sick, if you want. You can believe anything you want, it doesn't make it true. What's true is one company wins and everybody else gets fucked. That's what's true. Look at any space you want. You want to go back to your list? We can go through the list. Positioning has become sort of category design for the cowards. It's like, "Well, I know that we could really be as radical as to create our own space, so let's just see if we can carve off our little niche over here." Okay, great.
turns.zh: 嗯，那是事实正确。人们 go"哦，[听不清 01:18:21]。"好，所以你是说在科技里一家公司不拿三分之二经济？好，信那个。而你能信重力不存在。它存在，但你能信 Bigfoot 在 5G 塔上装喷雾器让我们都病，如果你要。你能信任何你要的，那不使它真。真的事是一家赢、其他所有人被 fuck。那是真的。看任何空间你要。你想回你清单？我们能走过清单。定位变成了某种给懦夫的品类设计。它像"嗯，我知道我们能真激进到创造自己的空间，所以就让看我们能不能在这切出我们的小 niche。"好，棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: A big part of positioning, just to expand on this a little bit, is differentiation. Differentiating yourself. People always talk about the importance of differentiation. Do you see that as the same potential pitfall, or how do you think about differentiation?
turns.zh: 定位很大一部份，就扩这点，是差异化。差异化你自己。人们总聊差异化的重要。你看那是同样的潜在陷阱吗，或者你怎么想差异化？

turns.speaker: Christopher Lochhead
turns.en: Okay, this is really, really powerful. In category design, we don't compete, period, full stop at the brand to brand or product to product level. Category designers do compete, but not against a product, not against a company, not against a brand. Category designers compete against the status quo. Let me be specific. There's a category called cycling. You look like you might be a biker, Lenny, are you?
turns.zh: 好，这真真强。在品类设计里，我们不在品牌对品牌或产品对产品层面竞争，句号、全停。品类设计者确实竞争，但不是对抗产品、不是对抗公司、不是对抗品牌。品类设计者对抗现状。让我具体。有个品类叫 cycling（骑行）。你看起来可能是个 biker，Lenny，是吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Very casually, mostly an e-bike.
turns.zh: 非常 casual，主要电助力。

turns.speaker: Christopher Lochhead
turns.en: Those are really fun.
turns.zh: 那些真有趣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: They're so fun. Mountain bike. Yeah.
turns.zh: 它们太有趣。山地车。对。

turns.speaker: Christopher Lochhead
turns.en: But you've been on a mountain bike. You've been on a road bike, you've gone out with friends, done this, right?
turns.zh: 但你骑过山地车。你骑过公路车，你跟朋友出去过、做过这个，对吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Christopher Lochhead
turns.en: Anybody who bikes on any kind of regular basis has been in an accident. And if you bike on a real regular basis, you've been in an accident with a vehicle that was not caused by you. That's true for every person I know that rides a bike on any regular basis, myself included. All of a sudden a new category shows up, and that new category is called indoor biking classes. And the category designer is a company called spinning. (01:20:53): And they say, "Hey, biking's great. It's an incredible source of exercise, but you don't want to get killed doing it, so come take a class." And what they're doing when they do that, they're competing category to category, not brand or product to brand. And that's a strategy that's called damming the demand. What does a dam do? There's a bunch of water running in the direction, a dam takes that water, stops it and moves it, does something to it. Interrupts it and changes it. Here's what spinning does. They say, "Why risk your life on a bike when you can take a wonderful class and not have to worry about it and get your exercise?" What dam the demand, Lenny, is you thought you wanted this, but what you really need is that. (01:21:52): Then what happens? The next iteration in that space comes from Peloton. Again, when Peloton launches, they don't say, "Hey, our bikes are better than spinning bikes. Our bikes are 12 mega flips, faster, cheaper." They don't do any of that shit. They don't shit on spinning, they don't attack spinning, they don't attack road biking, they don't do any of that stuff. They say, "Why drive to the gym when you could do it at home?" They dam the demand for spinning, they don't compete against it. And they reframe the problem called "How do I get a great workout in a group environment without getting killed?" And they achieve that massive success. (01:22:41): And I can give you many other examples. The mistake is competing directly product to product. The enemy is the status quo. That is to say the way it is now. If you go back to Lomi, the enemy, the way it is now, the status quo, is a nasty garbage in your kitchen that stinks and smells and gets all over the floor that you have to drag to the green bin and then the squirrels and the fucking raccoons eat it. That's the personal upset. And the environmental one is, we're destroying the planet. No, by the way, rather than destroy the planet, why not create this super awesome compost dirt? In category design, we call that a from to a Frodo. Category designers are leading the world from the way it is to a new and different way. They're not saying, "My carbide ingulator is better than their carbide ingulator." (01:23:32): Here's a simple example. This is another reason the word disrupt doesn't work. Les Paul is the innovator of the electric guitar. Today most guitar players have an electric guitar and an acoustic guitar. Matter of fact, most guitar players have more than one, very few guitar players, some, but very few said, "Oh, now that the electric guitar is invented, fuck the acoustic guitar." Very, very rare. The net new category called electric...
turns.zh: 任何以任何规律基础骑车的人都在事故里过。而如果你真规律地骑，你在不是你造成的、跟车的事故里过。那对我认识的每个任何规律基础骑车的人真——包括我。突然一个新品类出现，而那个新品类叫室内骑行课。而品类设计者是个叫 spinning 的公司。（01:20:53）而他们说"嘿，骑车很棒。它是锻炼的不可思议来源，但你不想骑死，所以来上课。"而他们做那个时在做的，是品类对品类竞争，不是品牌或产品对品牌。而那是个叫 damming the demand（筑坝需求）的战略。坝做什么？有一堆水朝一个方向流，坝拿那水、停它、移动它、对它做点啥。打断它、改它。这是 spinning 做的。他们说"你为啥冒死在车上，当你能上个好课、不用操心、拿到锻炼？"什么筑坝需求，Lenny，是你以为你要这个，但你真需要的是那个。（01:21:52）然后发生什么？那个空间的下个迭代来自 Peloton。再次，当 Peloton launch，他们不说"嘿，我们的车比 spinning 车好。我们的车 12 兆翻、更快、更便宜。"他们不做任何那 shit。他们不 shit on spinning、不攻击 spinning、不攻击公路骑行、不做任何那些。他们说"你为啥开车去健身房当你能在家做？"他们筑 spinning 的需求的坝，他们不跟它竞争。而他们重新框定了叫"我怎么在群体环境拿到好锻炼而不死？"的问题。而他们达成那个巨大成功。（01:22:41）而我能给很多其他例子。错是直接产品对产品竞争。敌人是现状。也就是现在的方式。如果你回 Lomi，敌人，现在的方式、现状，是厨房里恶心的、臭的、弄满地的垃圾，你得拖到绿箱然后松鼠和操的浣熊吃它。那是个人烦扰。而环境的是，我们在毁星球。不，顺带，与其毁星球，为啥不造这个超棒的堆肥土？在品类设计里，我们叫那 from to、一个 Frodo（故意搞笑拼错）。品类设计者领世界从现状到一个新的不同方式。他们不说"我的 carbide ingulator 比他们的 carbide ingulator 好。"（01:23:32）这是简单例子。这是另一个 disrupt 词不灵的原因。Les Paul 是电吉他的创新者。今天大多吉他手有电吉他和木吉他。事实上，大多吉他手有不止一个，很少吉他手、有些、但很少说"哦，现在电吉他发明了，操木吉他。"非常非常罕见。叫电吉他的全新品类，相对之前的品类木吉他，其实增加整体吉他 TAM。不颠覆 shit。所以在那案例，你其实在创造净新需求。在 Peloton 例子，你既创造那新需求又在得到你的开始。而这是我觉得你很多讨论、你很多关于增长的工作，Lenny，真强的地方，因为当增长管用时真正发生的是有效的数字筑坝需求。那是真正发生的，当它管用。

turns.speaker: Christopher Lochhead
turns.en: So the net new category called electric guitar as opposed to the prior category, acoustic guitar, actually increases the overall guitar TAM. Doesn't disrupt shit. So in that case, you're actually creating net new demand. In the Peloton example, you're both creating that new demand and you're getting your start. And this is where I think a lot of the discussion that you have and a lot of your work, Lenny, around growth, is really powerful, because what's really going on when growth works is effective digital damning of demand. That's what's really going on, when it works.
turns.zh: 我觉得某处也许写过，"Damn the TAM"是个超赞短语。如果你没，你该用那个。筑坝 TAM，增加 TAM。所以你有几本你出的书。我要链所有。Play Bigger，我想，是你的第一本，Niche Down 是另一本。而你最新的书，我相信是你最新的书，是《22 Laws of Category Design》（品类设计 22 律）。所以也许就作为最后一个问题，你能就分享几条这些律，也许两三你最爱的、从书里，给人一个书的感觉？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think somewhere maybe wrote this, "Damn the TAM" is an awesome phrase. If you haven't, you should use that. Damning the TAM, increasing the TAM. So you have a number of books you put out. I'm going to link to all these. Play Bigger, I think, was your first, Niche Down is the other. And your newest book, I believe is your newest book, is the 22 Laws of Category Design. So maybe just as a last question, can you just share a few of these laws, maybe two or three of your favorite laws from the book just to give people a sense of the book?
turns.zh: 我想我们聊了第一律，那在很多方面大概最重要。另一个要想的是我们叫 magic triangle（魔法三角）的东西，我们碰过，但也许没显式，也就是，为了建传奇公司，你得在对的时间把产品、公司、品类做对。所以有些人听品类设计讨论、觉得它某种贬低产品、好像产品不重要。品类设计的原因是因为我们爱产品。产品失败因为它们没被品类设计。所以我觉得 magic triangle 的 aha 是产品、公司、品类同等重要，所以做对那个我觉得很强。（01:26:05）我就是顶着我头 riff。我面前没它。另一个例子是 lightning strike（闪电袭击）vs peanut butter（花生酱）。所以大多营销人做的是，他们拿他们年营销预算，他们按季分，也许季度间有微差，但本质是类似金额花费。而他们做战役。他们做"keep the lights on（维持运转）"也许他们 launch 个产品、也许他们围绕产品有大推。而他们试图驱动漏斗、试图交付销售或交付线索，B2B，不重要。而那是他们做的。而他们没意识到，Lenny，那方法，那花生酱方法，基于几乎 100 年旧的心智脚手架和营销叫触达和频次（reach and frequency）。而触达和频次是关于，我想让我的 shit 在最多人面前最可能常。（01:27:07）而如果你听很多忽悠和 hustle porn 明星，那些 Gary V 之流，"你今天得在每个平台发 400 条内容。"所有这愚蠢。那只是触达频次从 50 多年前在新媒介的重拌。嗯，结果是触达频次不灵。因为我们收到的营销信息量巨大，有专家说我们一天收到多达 6 万，无论咖啡杯上 logo 还是网上广告和中间一切。所以几乎不可能在触达频次模式里脱颖而出。现在我不是说你不该做 keep the lights on 营销。你当然需要做维持运转营销。但，这是闪电袭击模型和品类设计教我们的。我宁愿一年就重要一周，也不要一年其他时间无关。（01:28:07）而我们做的，坦白 Lenny，是我们抄了 Hollywood launch 电影的模型。我们说"如果你作为软件公司做那个会怎样？如果你 launch 个东西，无论是产品还是别的，像 Hollywood launch 电影那样？"而所以闪电袭击是关于变得非常非常清楚，如果你回你 ICP 东西，"谁是我们理想客户？那客户在哪？她 hang out 哪？"理想，在数字世界先。你最近一期，我在听 Growth Hacker Gala，她怎么上 Reddit 和 shit。那是知名战略、我爱那战略。去他们 hang out 的地方，放点挑衅和吸引人的东西在他们面前，并在那刻重要。所以闪电袭击的想法是，如果我们是你那天或那两天的目标受众，我们会全在你身上。（01:29:09）我们会不可否认。所以我们放不成比例的努力，如果我们 B2B，大概一年一到两次闪电袭击。如果我们 B2C，两到三次。如果你真大公司，一季一次。小公司一季一次难搞。而比那多，如果不是闪电袭击，它开始糊回花生酱。但，那是很强概念。在执行侧对营销人，那不同。另一件我会说、也许该从这开始，所以我是三度上市公司 CMO。我顾问过 50 多家风投公司的品类设计和营销。猜我从没在营销计划里见过什么？

turns.speaker: Christopher Lochhead
turns.en: I think we talked about law number one, which, in a lot of ways, is probably the most important. Another one to think about is something we call the magic triangle, which we've touched on, but maybe not explicitly, which is, in order to build a legendary company, you've got to get product, company, and category right at the right time. And so some people hear the category design discussion and they think it's somehow pejorative to product as if product doesn't matter. The reason for category design is because we love the products. Products fail because they don't get category designed. So I think the aha of the magic triangle is product, company, and category are equal in importance, and so getting that right I think is very powerful. (01:26:05): I'm just riffing off the top of my head. I don't have it in front of me. Another example is lightning strikes versus peanut butter. So what most marketers do is they take their marketing budget for the year, they quarterize it, and maybe there's slight variance in the quarters, but essentially it's a similar amount of spend. And they do campaigns. And they do "keep the lights on" and maybe they launch a product and maybe they have a big push around the product. And they're trying to drive the funnel and they're trying to deliver sales or deliver leads, B2B, doesn't matter. And that's what they do. And what they don't realize, Lenny, is that approach, that peanut butter approach, is predicated on almost 100-year-old mental scaffolding and marketing called reach and frequency. And what reach and frequency was about, which was, I want to get my shit in front of the most amount of people the most often possible. (01:27:07): And if you listen to a lot of the shysters and hustle porn stars, the Gary VDs, and this is of the world, "You got to release 400 pieces of content today on every platform." All this stupidity. That's just a reswizzle of reach and frequency from over 50 years ago in the new medium. Well, it turns out reach and frequency doesn't work. Because the number of marketing messages we get is massive, they're experts who say we get up to 60,000 a day, whether it's logos on coffee cups or ads on the internet and everything in between. And so it's virtually impossible to stand out in a reach and frequency mode. Now I'm not saying you shouldn't be doing keep the lights on marketing. Of course you need to do keep the lights on marketing. But, here's what the lightning strike model and category design teaches us. I'd rather matter for one week a year than be irrelevant for the rest of the year. (01:28:07): And so what we did, candidly Lenny, was we ripped off Hollywood's model for launching movies. We said, "What if you did that as a software company? What if you launched a thing, be it a product or something else, the way Hollywood launches a movie?" And so what a lightning strike is about is getting very, very clear, if you go back to your ICP thing, "Who's our ideal customer? Where is that customer? Where does she hang out?" Ideally, in the digital world first. One of your recent episodes, I was listening to the Growth Hacker Gala, how she went on to Reddit and stuff. That's a well-known strategy and I love that strategy. Go hang out where they are, put something provocative and engaging in front of them, and matter in that moment. So the idea of a lightning strike is, if you are in our target audience for that day or that two days, we are going to be all over you. (01:29:09): We're going to be undeniable. And so we put a disproportionate amount of our effort, if we're in B2B, probably one to two lightning strikes a year. If we're in B2C, two to three. One a quarter if you're a really big company. It's hard to pull off one a quarter if you're a smaller company. And much more than that, if not a lightning strike, it starts to blur back into peanut butter. But, that is a very powerful concept. On the execution side for marketers, that's different. The other thing I'd say and probably should have started here, so I'm a three-time public company CMO. I've advised over 50 venture-backed companies in category design and marketing. Guess what I've never seen in a marketing plan ever?
turns.zh: 我想我们聊了第一律，那在很多方面大概最重要。另一个要想的是我们叫 magic triangle（魔法三角）的东西，我们碰过，但也许没显式，也就是，为了建传奇公司，你得在对的时间把产品、公司、品类做对。所以有些人听品类设计讨论、觉得它某种贬低产品、好像产品不重要。品类设计的原因是因为我们爱产品。产品失败因为它们没被品类设计。所以我觉得 magic triangle 的 aha 是产品、公司、品类同等重要，所以做对那个我觉得很强。（01:26:05）我就是顶着我头 riff。我面前没它。另一个例子是 lightning strike（闪电袭击）vs peanut butter（花生酱）。所以大多营销人做的是，他们拿他们年营销预算，他们按季分，也许季度间有微差，但本质是类似金额花费。而他们做战役。他们做"keep the lights on（维持运转）"也许他们 launch 个产品、也许他们围绕产品有大推。而他们试图驱动漏斗、试图交付销售或交付线索，B2B，不重要。而那是他们做的。而他们没意识到，Lenny，那方法，那花生酱方法，基于几乎 100 年旧的心智脚手架和营销叫触达和频次（reach and frequency）。而触达和频次是关于，我想让我的 shit 在最多人面前最可能常。（01:27:07）而如果你听很多忽悠和 hustle porn 明星，那些 Gary V 之流，"你今天得在每个平台发 400 条内容。"所有这愚蠢。那只是触达频次从 50 多年前在新媒介的重拌。嗯，结果是触达频次不灵。因为我们收到的营销信息量巨大，有专家说我们一天收到多达 6 万，无论咖啡杯上 logo 还是网上广告和中间一切。所以几乎不可能在触达频次模式里脱颖而出。现在我不是说你不该做 keep the lights on 营销。你当然需要做维持运转营销。但，这是闪电袭击模型和品类设计教我们的。我宁愿一年就重要一周，也不要一年其他时间无关。（01:28:07）而我们做的，坦白 Lenny，是我们抄了 Hollywood launch 电影的模型。我们说"如果你作为软件公司做那个会怎样？如果你 launch 个东西，无论是产品还是别的，像 Hollywood launch 电影那样？"而所以闪电袭击是关于变得非常非常清楚，如果你回你 ICP 东西，"谁是我们理想客户？那客户在哪？她 hang out 哪？"理想，在数字世界先。你最近一期，我在听 Growth Hacker Gala，她怎么上 Reddit 和 shit。那是知名战略、我爱那战略。去他们 hang out 的地方，放点挑衅和吸引人的东西在他们面前，并在那刻重要。所以闪电袭击的想法是，如果我们是你那天或那两天的目标受众，我们会全在你身上。（01:29:09）我们会不可否认。所以我们放不成比例的努力，如果我们 B2B，大概一年一到两次闪电袭击。如果我们 B2C，两到三次。如果你真大公司，一季一次。小公司一季一次难搞。而比那多，如果不是闪电袭击，它开始糊回花生酱。但，那是很强概念。在执行侧对营销人，那不同。另一件我会说、也许该从这开始，所以我是三度上市公司 CMO。我顾问过 50 多家风投公司的品类设计和营销。猜我从没在营销计划里见过什么？

turns.en: Word of mouth. This boggles our minds, those of us in category design, because WOM is was and always will be the most powerful form of marketing. So if you take the concept of a lightning strike, then you take the concept of a category point of view that is all about frame naming and claiming a problem. And then there's one other concept I'll introduce. (01:30:32): It sits next to your ideal customer profile. It's what in category design we call super consumers. So it turns out that in most categories, roughly eight to 10% of the buyers are responsible for the vast majority of the profits. And more importantly, they are the zeitgeist. They are the thought leaders in the industry. They are the customers, the users, the purveyors of whatever the thing is that others look up to as being the ones to admire, the ones to aspire to, the best practices, et cetera, et cetera. That's a super consumer. Okay. So in category design, when you understand who your supers are, i.e. your ideal customer profile, you understand where they are primarily in the native digital world, how do we go hang out? And remind me what that gal's name was? I thought she was awesome.
